newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FEATURE - Tropical diseases a burden for clean Singapore.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Tropical diseases a burden for clean Singapore.

text.p: Singapore may be one of the cleanest cities in the tropics, with stiff punishments for littering, spitting and not flushing the toilet, but it suffers unusually high death rates from some tropical diseases.
And, say medical experts, one major reason is because it is so heavily urbanised.
Clean-living standards help to minimise the risk, but some diseases are endemic and have little to do with hygiene, they say.

The mysterious and nasty Melioidosis, which kills more people in Singapore than malaria, cholera, chicken pox and dengue fever combined, is caused by a bacteria that thrives in wet soil, experts said.
MOSQUITO THRIVES IN URBAN JUNGLES
The mosquito, carrier of a wide variety of tropical fevers such as the sometimes deadly dengue, also thrives in the city.
The Aedes mosquito, which carries dengue, needs only a tiny pool of water in which to lay its eggs. In densely populated Singapore, researchers note, there are plenty of breeding places.
"Dengue fever doesn't necessarily affect slum environments, not like malaria. It can occur anywhere there is stagnant water the size of a 20-cent coin," said researcher Christina Liew.
Singapore has stepped up efforts to combat dengue and other mosquito-borne diseases such as malaria after suffering several epidemics over the last five years.
Last year a record 3,128 dengue fever cases were reported, compared with 1,983 cases in 1995, the Ministry of Environment said.
BREEDING SITES IN URBAN AREAS

Singapore says it has spent about $4.7 million (US$3.3 million) in recent years destroying breeding sites in its numerous public housing estates, in clogged drains and stagnant water in potted plants where the Aedes can lay eggs.
"It is because Singapore is so urbanised that it creates a problem. Some of these mosquitoes thrive in urban and domestic areas, in basically clean water," Liew said.
Dengue, also known as backbone fever, is a problem during the rainy season, which is normally towards the end of the year.
It causes high temperatures, headaches and pain in joints, and can occur in haemorrhagic form with internal bleeding.

Liew is studying how far the Aedes mosquito can fly and how a dengue outbreak occurs. This involves releasing about 50 mosquitoes ready to lay eggs -- their mouths clipped so they cannot transmit the fever by biting -- over a controlled site so their flight path can be charted.
Liew risks infection by letting mosquitoes bite her so she can trap them. "My aim is to catch them for identification, but you have to let them bite you first to catch them," she said.
It was not possible to know if mosquitoes are carrying the dengue virus until they can be dissected, she said.
CITY RESIDENTS HAVE LOW ANTI-BODIES
Melioidosis has proven more deadly in Singapore than in more rural areas of Southeast Asia because of low immunity levels among city people, experts say.
Authorities said anti-bodies were detected in only 0.2 percent of 1,854 people tested last year. In neighbouring countries the figure in similar tests is as high as 47 percent.

"The bacteria exist in many parts of the world but people in Southeast Asia generally are exposed and have immunity," Dr Kouichi Morita, Manila-based regional adviser in communicable diseases for the World Health Organisation, said.
Morita told Reuters that diagnosis was still difficult and the technique to isolate the bacteria was not available at many public health facilities in the region.
LITTLE ADVANCE TOWARD A CURE
Altogether 70 people got Melioidosis last year in Singapore, and 19 died. Since 1989, it has killed 147 people.
Blood poisoning, chest infection and abscesses are symptoms of the disease.
"The bacterium causing the disease may be present in water-logged soil and there are no effective ways of eradicating it," the ministry spokesman said.
He said the best that could be done was to detect and treat the disease as early as possible.
Workers in quarries, waste disposal, the zoo, sewage works and construction sites are most exposed to the disease, which attacks humans in different ways.
The germ is airborne but can also be ingested with comtaminated water or food or get into the blood through cuts, doctors said.
